Safeguards — monitoring and alerts

The guards that let monitoring deliver bad news — a four-signal health ladder shared by the page and the mailbox, workspace scoping, silent-unless-failing background work — and the catalog of alert signals.

👤 ForOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereMonitoring → Fleet health; Jobs; Settings → Alerts (thresholds, recipients, cooldown)
On this page
  • Monitoring that can say no
  • The alert catalog

Monitoring that can say no#

A monitoring page earns its place by being able to deliver bad news. Several of these guards exist because a screen was structurally incapable of it.

Guard What it prevents
The health badge grades four signals A badge that can never turn red. Scoring only on capacity headroom meant an appliance that was powered off, whose harvest had failed for days and which had nothing cached still rendered healthy. Harvest, cache age, probes and capacity are now graded together, and every failing signal is printed on the card.
unknown ranks below ok Absence of measurement reading as health. A device about which nothing has been measured shows unknown, never healthy.
A disabled probe is not a passing probe Silencing a monitor to clear a board. Switching a probe off removes coverage, and the card says so.
The page and the mailbox share one ladder Two surfaces disagreeing. Before this, the alert side was a bare network probe — appliances answered their port for a week with a dead harvest and never produced a single mail.
A page load never opens a connection to an appliance A monitoring screen that hangs when the thing it monitors is down. Every view is served from the database; probing is a background sweep or an explicit action.
A workspace never shows the manager's infrastructure Node names and infrastructure addresses appearing inside a product view. The data endpoints omit those sections outside the manager workspace and the infrastructure routes answer 403 — a hidden card whose endpoint still answers is hidden, not scoped.
Fleet-wide actions resolve their targets in the request A sweep launched from one product workspace opening connections to appliances of another. Worker threads have no workspace of their own, so the target list is resolved where it exists and passed in.
Absence of data is never health A zero transaction count on a saturated service. A zero is cross-checked against live sessions before it may grade healthy; an empty bucket list is an error; a watched port that disappears is named, not dropped from a shorter list.
Recurring work is silent unless it fails Alert fatigue from the system announcing that it is doing what it was told. A sweep raises nothing on success — and a failure is the one thing the page itself cannot show, because stale numbers look current. Silent work still appears in full on the Jobs page.
Stale work is swept out of the progress feed A control the operator cannot use. An abandoned task offering a Stop button that can never work teaches people that the progress area lies — and then the one that matters is dismissed too.
The test suite cannot write to the live job ledger Running the tests on a node inventing phantom background tasks in production — which is what kept reappearing every time the product was worked on: running the tests to verify a change was itself producing the noise the change removed.
Parked appliances are skipped, not failed A permanent critical alert about machines nobody expects to answer. A run whose entire target set is in maintenance reports skipped, which does not feed a failure streak; a manual run still reaches them.

💡Tip

The four health signals and their thresholds are described in Device health. Probes are covered in Probes and Deep monitors.

The alert catalog#

All of the above is only useful if silence means healthy. Thresholds and recipients live in Settings; each signal has its own cooldown. Delivery (in-app bell, e-mail, signed webhook, integration hooks and syslog) is described in Alerting.

Signal Fires when
Certificate expiry / error The service certificate is inside the warning window, or cannot be read.
Renewal failed A renewal attempt failed — critical from three consecutive failures.
Unpushed commits Local history has been waiting too long to reach the remote.
Behind / diverged The checkout trails the remote past the limit, or both sides have moved.
Backup missing / stale / error There is no backup at all, none recent enough, or the check itself failed.
Device health An appliance is degraded or critical on the same four-signal ladder the page uses — one finding per device, with every failing signal as a line in the message — plus a live network probe that the page deliberately does not have.
Device error The appliance list, or one device's health roll-up, could not be read at all.
Scheduled action failing A scheduled run has failed repeatedly. Only scheduled runs count — a manual run is already on someone's screen, and mixing them would hide the case where the scheduled path is broken while manual runs pass.
Scheduled action overdue An enabled action whose next run came and went. Without this, a dead scheduler looks perfectly healthy — it produces no failed runs to count.
Drift error The configuration drift comparison could not run.
Engine error The alert engine itself failed — the guard on the guard.

ℹ️Note — More signals in the current release

The engine also raises: Git status unreadable (ahead/behind could not be measured, so they are not reported as healthy zeros); Config drift on a device when a device's harvested configuration changed without a recorded SATOM write (a change SATOM did make is reported as made through SATOM); Host degraded / critical for disk, memory or load on a SATOM node; Signature DB stale / unreadable for appliances whose signature database stopped updating; and catalog findings about object disappearances and catalog paths that look wrong for a firmware line. See Alerting.

❗Important — Severity is part of the quiet-period key

A device or action that degrades from warning to critical inside the cooldown still reaches the operator — a fixed key would suppress precisely the escalation the alert exists for. A finding is filed under the workspace of the appliance, never the session that happened to compute it, so a load-balancer alarm never rings in the firewall workspace.

#fleet health#health badge#unknown#probe#disabled probe#cooldown#severity#workspace#adom#scoping#background job#maintenance#parked#alert catalog#signals#unpushed commits#backup#scheduled action#overdue#drift
